claims.text: A combined high-throughput MD and CALPHAD framework can accurately determine melting temperatures for high-entropy alloys.
The framework can accurately determine enthalpies of fusion for high-entropy alloys.
The framework can accurately determine entropies of fusion for high-entropy alloys.
The framework can accurately determine volume changes at melting for high-entropy alloys.
The framework can accurately determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for high-entropy alloys.
The combined framework will provide an efficient, high-throughput alternative for screening broad compositional spaces.
A typical high-entropy-alloy solid solution contains 4–8 principal elements with randomized site occupancy.
A modeled homogeneous randomized solid solution reflects as-cast or homogenized experimental high-entropy-alloy microstructures.
Atomic-scale free-energy landscapes and solid–liquid interfacial configurations mediate extraction of latent heat, entropy change, and volume change.
Thermodynamic integration along suitable transformation pathways computes free-energy differences between solid and liquid phases.
Combining MD trajectories and atomic-level information with CALPHAD models yields macroscopic thermodynamic properties.
Accurate sampling of configurational space and phase-coexistence configurations enables precise determination of latent thermodynamic parameters.
Predicted melting temperatures will agree with experiment within approximately 10–20% error.
Predicted fusion enthalpies will agree with experiment within approximately 10–20% error.
Predicted fusion entropies will agree with experiment within approximately 10–20% error.
The framework will capture thermodynamic trends across different high-entropy-alloy compositions.
Traditional calorimetry, dilatometry, and high-temperature microscopy are accurate but low-throughput and less comprehensive for wide compositional screening.
The method is most applicable to high-entropy alloys that approximate solution behavior.
Significant short-range order, phase segregation, or non-ideal mixing may place an alloy outside the reliable predictive regime of the selected interatomic potentials.
